title: What should you ask first in a product improvement case, and which trap should you avoid?
description: The first question to ask in a product improvement or growth case, how to structure it, and the trap to avoid.
hook: Ask first which measure the improvement should move (engagement, retention, revenue or satisfaction), because "make it better" has no answer until you know what better means. The trap is defaulting to the biggest user group instead of choosing the group whose problem matters most to the goal.
body:
The first question to ask

Improve it on which measure, and for whom?

"How would you improve our music app?" could mean more new users, more listening per user, fewer cancellations or more paid subscribers. Each one points to a different user group and a different set of fixes. Ask what the business cares about most right now, then confirm the product's mission: what it is for, and why people use it.

"I'd like to focus on one group of users rather than everyone. Which matters most to the business right now: new users, or keeping existing ones?"

How to build your structure

  1. Start from the product's mission.
  2. Pick one user group and one use case.
  3. Walk their journey and find the friction.
  4. Suggest solutions.
  5. Rank by impact against effort (the 80/20 rule helps here).
  6. Choose a success metric, plus a guardrail metric that must not get worse.

The wider growth tree is in the growth strategy framework.

Worked example: adoption before engagement

A learning platform wants 30% more weekly active users. That number can rise because more people start using the product or because existing users come back more often. Split it before suggesting anything.

Suppose 100,000 people sign up each month, but only 20% finish the first lesson. Walking the new user's journey shows where they get stuck: a long sign-up form and a placement test before any learning. Say a shorter onboarding lifts completion to 30%.

Per monthly cohortBeforeAfter
Finish first lesson (20% → 30%)20,00030,000
Still weekly active after a month (40%)8,00012,000
Buy a $120 annual plan (5% of activated)$120k$180k

Activated users rise 50% with no change in sign-ups. The 40% and 5% rates are assumptions to test: if users who skip the placement test drop out later, the gain shrinks. So run it as an experiment, with guardrails such as refund requests and course completion. More notifications might lift opens this week and hurt retention next month; good product growth means value that lasts.

The trap most people fall into

Defaulting to the biggest user group. "Everyone" or "our main users" sounds safe but leads to generic ideas. The right group is the one whose friction most limits the goal. Here, that is new users in their first week, not loyal learners.

Weak: "I'd add social features, gamification and a dark mode for all users."
Strong: "Most sign-ups never finish lesson one, so I'd focus on new users' first session. Cutting onboarding to one screen could lift activation from 20% to 30%. I'd test it, and watch refunds and completion as guardrails."

Two prompts to try

How would you improve a music streaming app?

Show the answer
  • Goal: for example, more listening hours per user.
  • User: new listeners in their first week.
  • Friction: they cannot quickly find music they like.
  • Ideas: a better first-day playlist from a few taps of taste; importing favourites from another app.
  • Measure: listening hours in week one; guardrail: existing listeners' satisfaction with recommendations.

The trap: redesigning for heavy users who already love it.

How would you grow paid subscriptions for a meditation app?

Show the answer
  • Funnel: free users × share who start a trial × share who pay after the trial.
  • User: free users who meditate several times a week but have not trialled, since they already see value.
  • Friction: unclear what paying adds; trial asks for card details up front.
  • Ideas: show a locked course after the fifth session; a trial without card details.
  • Measure: trial-to-paid conversion; guardrail: free-user retention.

The trap: discounting the price before knowing which step of the funnel leaks.
